1.1: Solomon, David's son, got solid in his role as king. The Lord his God was with him heavy, and God lifted him up real high in the eyes of the people.
1.2: He hollered at all of Israel—the generals over thousands and hundreds, the judges, and all the big-name folks from the tribes and families.
1.3: Then Solomon and the whole squad went to the high place in Gibeon. That's where the tent of meeting—the one Moses built in the wilderness—was still standing.
1.4: But David had already brought the Ark of God up from Kiriath-Jearim to Jerusalem, where he had set up a special tent for it.
1.5: Now the bronze altar that Bezalel (the son of Uri, son of Hur) made, that was still up front at the Tabernacle. So Solomon and the whole crowd went there to seek God.
1.6: Solomon stepped up to the bronze altar in front of the Lord's tabernacle and sacrificed a thousand burnt offerings on it. That's some next-level worship.
1.7: That night, God pulled up on Solomon in a dream and said, 'Go ahead, ask for whatever you want—I got you.'
1.8: Solomon said, 'Lord, you really showed love to my pops, David. And now you done made me king in his place.'
1.9: 'So now, Lord God, please make good on the promise you made to David, 'cause you done made me king over a people that can't even be counted—like dust on the ground!'
1.10: 'I need wisdom and know-how, God. Help me lead your people right. 'Cause who else could handle a crew this big and important?'
1.11: God said, 'You know what, since you ain't ask for money, fame, revenge, or a long life—but you asked for wisdom and knowledge to lead my people right? I got you.'
1.12: 'I'ma give you that wisdom and knowledge. But on top of that, I'ma throw in the riches, wealth, and honor too—more than any king before you or after you will ever have.'
1.13: Then Solomon left Gibeon—the place of worship—and went back to Jerusalem to start reigning full-time as king of Israel.
1.14: He started collecting chariots and horses—1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen. He kept 'em posted in the chariot cities and some in Jerusalem right by him.
1.15: Solomon had silver and gold all over Jerusalem—it was like having pebbles in the street. And he had cedar trees stacked like regular sycamores in the lowlands.
1.16: Dude had horses brought in from Egypt and Keveh, with the royal dealers buyin' them at market price like it was nothing.
1.17: A chariot from Egypt ran you 600 shekels of silver, and a horse? 150. Solomon's crew was running export deals too—flipping chariots and horses to kings of the Hittites and Syria.

2.1: Solomon had his mind made up—he was gon' build a temple to rep the name of the Lord, and a royal crib for himself too.
2.2: He picked out 70,000 workers to carry the heavy stuff, 80,000 stonecutters to get the rock out the mountains, and 3,600 supervisors to keep everything in check.
2.3: Solomon hit up Hiram, the king of Tyre, sayin', 'Just like you came through for my daddy David with them cedar logs for his house, I need you to come through for me too.'
2.4: 'I'm buildin' a temple in the name of the Lord my God. It's gon' be where we burn sweet incense for Him, keep the showbread on deck, and offer up burnt sacrifices—every morning, every night, on the Sabbaths, New Moons, and all the Lord's holy days. This ain't no one-time thing—this forever for Israel.'
2.5: 'This temple I'm buildin'? It's gon' be somethin' serious, 'cause our God bigger and greater than any other out there.'
2.6: 'But for real, who can even build a house for God? Not even heaven or the heavens beyond heaven can hold Him. So who am I to think I can build Him a place—except just to offer sacrifices?'
2.7: 'So do me a favor—send me somebody who knows what they doin'. I'm talkin' a master craftsman, good with gold, silver, bronze, and iron, who can also work with purple, crimson, and blue fabrics. Somebody who knows how to do engravings and work alongside the skilled brothers my pops, David, already set up in Judah and Jerusalem.'
2.8: 'And send cedar, cypress, and algum wood from Lebanon, 'cause your people know how to chop timber like nobody else. My folks gon' work with your folks on this.'
2.9: 'We need a whole lotta wood, 'cause this temple I'm about to build? It's gon' be grand and straight-up jaw-dropping.'
2.10: 'And I got y'all—your lumber crew gon' eat good. I'm sendin' twenty thousand kors of wheat, twenty thousand kors of barley, twenty thousand baths of wine, and twenty thousand baths of oil for 'em.'
2.11: Then King Hiram hit Solomon back with a letter sayin', 'The Lord must really love His people, 'cause He blessed y'all with you as king.'
2.12: He added, 'Shoutout to the Lord, the God of Israel—Creator of heaven and earth! He gave David a wise and smart son, somebody with real insight, who can build a temple for the Lord and a palace for himself. That's big!'
2.13: 'I'm sendin' you a top-tier craftsman named Huram, one of my best men.'
2.14: 'His mama's from the tribe of Dan and his pops from Tyre. Dude got skills with gold, silver, bronze, iron, stone, and wood. He know how to work with purple, blue, fine linen, and crimson too. He can engrave anything and execute any design you give him. He'll work side by side with your squad and the same talented folks your daddy David put on.'
2.15: 'So go ahead and send that wheat, barley, oil, and wine you promised—my people ready for it.'
2.16: 'We'll cut all the wood you need from Lebanon and float it down the coast to Joppa. From there, your folks can haul it up to Jerusalem.'
2.17: Then Solomon took a fresh census of all the foreigners livin' in Israel, just like his daddy David had done. Turned out there were 153,600 of 'em.
2.18: He put 70,000 of them to carry loads, 80,000 to work the stone in the hills, and 3,600 bosses to keep the work movin' smooth.

3.1: Solomon kicked off the buildin' of the Lord's house in Jerusalem, right up on Mount Moriah. That's the same spot where God showed up to his daddy David. David had already picked out the place—it was the threshin' floor that used to belong to Ornan the Jebusite.
3.2: He broke ground on the second day of the second month, in the fourth year of his reign.
3.3: Here's how he laid the foundation: the temple was sixty cubits long and twenty cubits wide, using the old-school measurements.
3.4: Up front, the entry hall stretched twenty cubits wide and stood one hundred and twenty cubits high. The whole inside was layered in pure gold—no shortcuts.
3.5: The main room got that cypress wood paneling, and Solomon covered it in fine gold. He carved in palm trees and a chain pattern to give it that holy drip.
3.6: He threw in precious stones all around to make it shine, and the gold came straight from Parvaim—a high-end spot.
3.7: Even the beams, doorframes, walls, and doors got covered in gold. And he didn't stop there—he carved cherubim (angel figures) into the walls too.
3.8: Then he built the Most Holy Place, a perfect square—twenty cubits long and twenty cubits wide. He layered that spot with six hundred talents worth of fine gold. That's crazy rich.
3.9: Even the nails? Pure gold. Each one weighed fifty shekels. The upper areas? Gold-covered too.
3.10: Inside that Holy of Holies, Solomon had two carved cherubim set up, all gold everything.
3.11: Each cherub had two wings—one wing stretched five cubits to the wall, the other wing reached out five cubits to touch the other cherub.
3.12: Same for the second cherub—five cubits one way to the wall, five cubits the other way to the first cherub's wing.
3.13: So both wings stretched out a full twenty cubits across the room. The cherubim stood upright, facing forward.
3.14: He made a veil too—real intricate, with blue, purple, crimson, and fine linen, and he had cherubim woven into it.
3.15: Out front, Solomon put up two tall pillars—thirty-five cubits high. Each one had a top piece, called a capital, that was five cubits.
3.16: He made decorative chain designs like the ones inside and put those on the pillar tops. Then he added a hundred gold pomegranates to the chains—details mattered.
3.17: He set the pillars at the temple entrance—one on the right side, one on the left. The right one he named Jachin, the left one he called Boaz.

4.1: Solomon made a big ol' bronze altar—it was twenty cubits long, twenty wide, and ten cubits high. That joint was massive.
4.2: Then he crafted the Sea—a huge round basin made of cast bronze. It was ten cubits across, five cubits tall, and thirty cubits all the way around.
4.3: Under the rim, it had these bronze ox figures all around it—ten per cubit, two rows total, all part of the same mold when they poured the bronze.
4.4: The whole Sea sat on twelve bronze oxen—three lookin' north, three west, three south, and three east. Their backs were to the center, and the Sea sat right on top of 'em.
4.5: The thing was thick too—a handbreadth thick—and the rim was shaped like a cup, flarin' out like a lily blossom. It could hold about 3,000 baths of water.
4.6: He made ten smaller wash basins too. Five went on the right side and five on the left. They used those to clean up whatever they were sacrificin'—but the Sea? That was just for the priests to wash in.
4.7: Solomon made ten golden lampstands, stickin' to the original design. He set five on the right and five on the left inside the temple.
4.8: He made ten tables too—again, five on each side. Then he added one hundred gold bowls to match.
4.9: He didn't stop there—he built the courtyard for the priests, the big outer court, and the doors for it too. Covered those doors in bronze.
4.10: He placed the big Sea on the southeast corner of the temple courtyard.
4.11: Huram—the craftsman Solomon hired—finished his work. He made the pots, the shovels, the bowls, and all the extra gear for God's house.
4.12: That included the two massive pillars, the rounded tops (called capitals) on each one, and the two intricate networks of chain design that covered those tops.
4.13: He also made 400 bronze pomegranates—two rows for each chain network to decorate the top of the pillars.
4.14: Huram built carts too, with lavers (those smaller water basins) mounted on 'em.
4.15: He made one giant Sea, and put twelve bronze oxen under it to hold it up.
4.16: And all the utensils—pots, shovels, forks—Huram made 'em all outta polished bronze for King Solomon to use in the temple.
4.17: They poured all that bronze work in clay molds out in the Jordan Valley, between Succoth and Zeredah.
4.18: Solomon had so much bronze stuff made, nobody even tried to weigh it—it was that much.
4.19: Solomon got all the furnishings for God's house made—the gold altar, the tables for the showbread.
4.20: The gold lampstands too, with their lamps, all burnin' the way God laid it out, placed in front of the inner sanctuary.
4.21: He made flowers, lamps, and wick trimmers—all pure gold, top quality.
4.22: He finished it off with gold trimmers, bowls, ladles, and incense burners. Even the doors for the sanctuary and the Most Holy Place? All of 'em were covered in gold.

5.1: Once Solomon finished everything for the Lord's house, he brought in all the stuff his father David had set aside—gold, silver, all the sacred furniture—and stored it in the treasuries of God's house.
5.2: Then Solomon called a big gathering in Jerusalem—he brought together all the elders, tribe leaders, and heads of the families of Israel. The goal? To bring up the Ark of the Covenant from the City of David (that's Zion).
5.3: So all the men of Israel showed up during the feast in the seventh month, standing with the king.
5.4: The elders came through, and the Levites got ready to carry the Ark.
5.5: They brought up the Ark, the tent of meeting, and all the holy items that were inside it. The priests and the Levites were the ones carryin' it all.
5.6: Solomon and the whole crowd of Israelites gathered around the Ark, sacrificin' so many sheep and oxen, they couldn't even keep count. That's how deep the worship ran.
5.7: Then the priests took the Ark of the Covenant into the inner sanctuary of the temple—the Most Holy Place—and placed it under the wings of the cherubim.
5.8: The cherubim had their wings stretched out over the spot, coverin' the Ark and its carrying poles.
5.9: Those poles were so long, the ends could be seen from the main holy room—but not from outside. And they still there to this day.
5.10: Inside the Ark was only the two stone tablets Moses put in back at Horeb, when the Lord made His covenant with Israel after they came outta Egypt.
5.11: Now when the priests came outta the Most Holy Place, all of 'em had already purified themselves. Didn't matter what division they were from—they all made sure they were clean.
5.12: And the Levite singers—Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, along with their sons and crew—stood on the east side of the altar, dressed in white linen. They had cymbals, harps, and stringed instruments, and 120 priests were blowin' trumpets.
5.13: When the trumpeters and singers linked up like one voice, all in sync, givin' praise and thanks to the Lord, they turned it all the way up. They lifted their voices, blew the trumpets, banged the cymbals, and played every instrument they had. The whole place echoed with: 'The Lord is good, His mercy lasts forever!' And just like that, the temple got filled with a thick cloud.
5.14: The priests couldn't even do their duties after that—the cloud was too heavy. That was the glory of the Lord movin' in and fillin' His house.

6.1: Then Solomon said, 'The Lord said He'd live in thick darkness.'
6.2: 'But look, I done built You a high and holy house, Lord—a place for You to live in forever.'
6.3: Then Solomon turned around and blessed everybody in the assembly of Israel. They was all standin' there.
6.4: He said, 'Bless the Lord, the God of Israel! He did exactly what He told my daddy David He would do—spoke it with His mouth, made it happen with His hands.'
6.5: 'Ever since God brought our people outta Egypt, He ain't picked no city in Israel for a temple, and He ain't picked no man to rule the people—'
6.6: '—but now He picked Jerusalem for His name to dwell, and He chose David to lead Israel.'
6.7: 'My pops, David, had it in his heart to build a temple for God's name.'
6.8: 'And God told him, "That's beautiful, David. I see your heart, and it's in the right place."'
6.9: 'But God also told him, "You ain't the one to build it—your son will. Your own blood will build My temple."'
6.10: 'So now, here I am. I'm sittin' on David's throne, just like God said would happen. And I built the temple for the name of the Lord, the God of Israel.'
6.11: 'I even put the Ark in there—the same Ark with the covenant God made with our people when He brought us outta Egypt.'
6.12: Solomon stepped up to the altar in front of the whole crowd of Israel, raised his hands up toward heaven—
6.13: (He had set up a bronze platform in the middle of the courtyard—five cubits wide, five cubits deep, and three high. He stood on it, dropped to his knees in front of everybody, and raised his hands to the sky.)
6.14: He said, 'Lord, God of Israel, there ain't nobody like You—in heaven or on earth. You keep Your promises and show love to those who walk with You with a real heart.'
6.15: 'You kept Your word to my father David. What You said with Your mouth, You backed up with action. And look—it's done.'
6.16: 'Now Lord, keep that same energy. You told David, "As long as your sons walk right with Me, there'll always be one of y'all on the throne of Israel."'
6.17: 'So now, God of Israel, let that word You spoke come true.'
6.18: 'But hold up—can God really live here on earth with us? Even the highest heavens can't hold You. So how this little temple gon' do it?'
6.19: 'Still, Lord, hear my prayer. Hear my cry. I'm layin' it all out before You.'
6.20: 'Keep Your eyes on this temple day and night—this is where You said You'd put Your name. So when I pray toward this place, hear me out.'
6.21: 'And when Your people pray toward this spot, hear us from heaven, where You really live—and when You hear, forgive us.'
6.22: 'If someone wrongs somebody else and they swear their case at this altar—'
6.23: 'Lord, judge it right. Make the guilty take the L and clear the name of the one who did right.'
6.24: 'If Israel get beat by enemies 'cause we sinned, but then we turn back, call on Your name, and pray at this temple—'
6.25: 'Please hear us from heaven, forgive us, and bring us back to the land You gave our people.'
6.26: 'If the skies dry up and there's no rain 'cause of our sins, but then we pray toward this place, confess, and turn from our ways—'
6.27: 'Then hear from heaven, forgive, and teach us the right path. Bless the land You gave us with rain again.'
6.28: 'If there's famine, disease, mildew, locusts, or enemy attacks—whatever the crisis is—'
6.29: 'If folks cry out to You, each one knowin' their own struggle, and they stretch their hands toward this temple—'
6.30: 'Hear 'em, Lord. From Your heavenly home, hear and forgive. Handle each one's situation based on what You know about their heart—'cause only You really know what's in folks' hearts.'
6.31: 'That way, they'll respect You and walk in Your ways the whole time they live in this land You gave our ancestors.'
6.32: 'And even when a foreigner—somebody who ain't from Israel—shows up 'cause they heard about Your greatness, and they pray toward this temple—'
6.33: 'Please hear them too, Lord. Answer their prayer, so the whole world will know Your name and respect You like we do. Let 'em know this house got Your name on it.'
6.34: 'When we go out to war where You send us, and we pray toward this city and this temple—'
6.35: 'Hear us from heaven and fight for us.'
6.36: 'Now we know we gon' mess up sometimes—ain't nobody perfect. If You let us get captured and taken away to a foreign land—'
6.37: 'But if we come to our senses, repent, and cry out to You sayin', "We messed up, Lord"—'
6.38: 'And if we turn back to You with all we got, and pray toward this land, this city, and this temple—'
6.39: 'Then please hear us from Your place in heaven. Listen to our prayers, stand up for us, and forgive us for everything we did wrong.'
6.40: 'Now, my God, I'm askin'—let Your eyes be open and Your ears tuned in to every prayer made right here.'
6.41: 'Lord God, rise up and come rest in this place—You and the Ark that shows Your power. Let Your priests be draped in salvation, and let Your people turn up with joy and goodness.'
6.42: 'And Lord, don't turn Your back on Your chosen one. Remember all the love You showed Your servant David.'

7.1: As soon as Solomon finished his prayer, boom!—fire came down from heaven and lit up the burnt offering and all the sacrifices. God's glory filled up the whole temple.
7.2: It was so thick in there, the priests couldn't even step inside. God's presence had the whole place on lock.
7.3: When everybody in Israel saw that fire drop and the glory sittin' heavy on the temple, they fell on their faces right on the pavement. They worshiped and shouted out loud: 'The Lord is good! His mercy lasts forever!'
7.4: Then the king and the whole crowd brought sacrifices to the Lord.
7.5: Solomon went big with it—he sacrificed 22,000 bulls and 120,000 sheep. The king and the people dedicated God's house for real.
7.6: The priests did their part, stayin' on duty. The Levites were posted too, playin' the instruments David made for worship. Every time they played and praised, they sang, 'His mercy lasts forever!' The priests blew the trumpets across from them, and all Israel stood in unity.
7.7: Solomon even made the middle of the courtyard holy, the part in front of the temple. That's where he had to offer up more burnt offerings and peace offerings. The bronze altar he made wasn't big enough to handle all that—they had to expand.
7.8: They threw a feast for seven days—everybody in Israel came through, from Hamath in the north to the Brook of Egypt in the south. Big crowd.
7.9: On the eighth day, they held a special gathering, 'cause the altar dedication took seven days, and the feast ran the full seven too.
7.10: By the 23rd day of the seventh month, Solomon sent everybody home. Folks left feelin' good—full of joy 'cause of what the Lord had done for David, for Solomon, and for His people.
7.11: With that, Solomon wrapped up the temple and his own palace. Everything he set out to do in both houses was a success.
7.12: Later on, God showed up to Solomon at night and said, 'I heard your prayer. I've picked this place as My house of sacrifice.'
7.13: 'If I shut the skies and stop the rain, or if I call in locusts to eat up the crops, or send disease among My people—'
7.14: 'If My people, the ones called by My name, humble themselves, pray, seek Me, and turn from their mess—then I'll hear from heaven, forgive their sins, and heal their land.'
7.15: 'Now My eyes wide open, and My ears tuned in to every prayer made in this place.'
7.16: 'I've chosen this temple and made it holy. My name's stamped here forever, and I'ma keep My eyes and My heart on it always.'
7.17: 'And you, Solomon—if you walk with Me like your father David did, and keep My laws and do what I told you—'
7.18: 'Then I'ma keep your kingdom solid, just like I promised David. You'll always have someone from your line ruling over Israel.'
7.19: 'But if you flip the script, turn away from Me, and start worshipin' other gods—'
7.20: 'I'ma pull y'all up outta this land I gave you. And this house I made holy? I'll throw it outta My sight. Folks gon' look at it and use it as a punchline.'
7.21: 'Even though this house is glorious now, later on, people gon' walk by and be like, "What happened here? Why'd the Lord do this to His own place?"'
7.22: 'And the answer gon' be: "Because they turned their backs on the Lord, the God of their ancestors—the same one who brought 'em outta Egypt. They ran off to worship fake gods, so He let the disaster hit 'em."'

8.1: So after twenty years—after Solomon had finished building both the Lord's temple and his own crib—
8.2: He started fixing up the cities that Hiram had given him. He rebuilt them and moved some Israelites in.
8.3: Solomon also rolled up to Hamath Zobah and took it over—straight conquest mode.
8.4: He built up Tadmor in the desert too, along with all his storage cities in Hamath.
8.5: He stacked up Upper and Lower Beth Horon with strong walls, gates, and heavy-duty bars.
8.6: He built up Baalath and all his supply cities, chariot cities, cavalry cities—anything he felt like buildin' in Jerusalem, Lebanon, or anywhere else he ruled.
8.7: Now the leftover folks from the Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites—the ones Israel hadn't wiped out—
8.8: Solomon put their descendants on work duty. That was the labor crew, and that's how it stayed.
8.9: But Solomon ain't make Israelites do forced labor. His people held it down as soldiers, officers, chariot commanders, and cavalry leaders.
8.10: He also had 250 top officials who were runnin' point over all the people.
8.11: Solomon moved Pharaoh's daughter outta the City of David into the house he built just for her. He said, 'She can't stay where the Ark of the Lord was—those places are holy.'
8.12: Then Solomon kept up with offerin' burnt sacrifices to the Lord on the altar he built in front of the temple's entrance.
8.13: He followed the schedule Moses gave: daily offerings, Sabbaths, New Moons, and the three major feasts—Unleavened Bread, Weeks, and Tabernacles.
8.14: Solomon also kept his daddy David's system in place: priests did their duties, Levites sang and served, and gatekeepers stayed posted by the doors. Everybody had their assigned spot.
8.15: They followed every instruction from the king—nothing got skipped. Even the treasury rules stayed locked in.
8.16: Solomon's whole project—from day one of the foundation to the finishing touches—was done right. The Lord's temple was officially complete.
8.17: After that, Solomon went down to Ezion Geber and Elath on the coast of Edom.
8.18: Hiram sent ships and skilled sailors from his crew to link up with Solomon's. They sailed to Ophir and brought back 450 talents of gold for King Solomon.

9.1: When the Queen of Sheba heard all about Solomon's fame, she pulled up to Jerusalem to see if the hype was real. She came deep—with a whole squad, camels loaded with spices, a crazy amount of gold, and precious gems. She brought Solomon all her questions—straight from the heart.
9.2: Solomon answered every single one. Nothing was too deep or too hard for him to break down.
9.3: When she saw all his wisdom, the palace he built—
9.4: —the food on the table, how his staff was sittin', the servers in their uniforms, the cupbearers fresh, even the hallway he used to walk up to the Lord's temple—she was shook. Straight speechless.
9.5: She told the king, 'Everything I heard back home about you and your wisdom? It was true.'
9.6: 'I ain't believe it at first. But now that I've seen it for myself? Man, they didn't even tell me half of it. You go beyond everything they said.'
9.7: 'Your people blessed. Your servants blessed—'cause they get to stand in front of you and soak up your wisdom all day.'
9.8: 'Praise the Lord your God, who clearly loves you and your people. That's why He made you king—to hold it down with justice and righteousness.'
9.9: Then she gave Solomon 120 talents of gold, more spices than they'd ever seen, and a pile of precious stones. Ain't nobody ever brought spices like she did.
9.10: Also, Hiram's and Solomon's crews brought in more gold from Ophir, plus algum wood and gems.
9.11: The king used that algum wood to build walkways for God's house and his own house, and even made harps and stringed instruments for the singers. Judah had never seen instruments like that before.
9.12: Solomon didn't let her leave empty-handed. He gave the Queen of Sheba everything she asked for—and then some. After that, she headed back to her land with her people.
9.13: Every year Solomon was stackin'—666 talents of gold came in annually.
9.14: That didn't even count what the traders, merchants, Arabian kings, and local governors brought to him in gold and silver.
9.15: Solomon made 200 big shields from hammered gold—each one took 600 shekels.
9.16: Then he made 300 smaller shields—300 shekels each. All of them got stored in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
9.17: The king had a throne made outta ivory and covered it in pure gold.
9.18: It had six steps, a gold footstool, armrests on both sides, and two lions posted up beside the armrests.
9.19: Then there were twelve more lions—one at the end of each step on both sides. Nobody in any other kingdom had a throne like that.
9.20: All his cups were gold. Everything in that Forest House was gold—silver was considered cheap back then.
9.21: His ships teamed up with Hiram's and went to Tarshish. Every three years they'd come back with gold, silver, ivory, apes, and monkeys.
9.22: Solomon outshined every king on earth in both wealth and wisdom.
9.23: Kings from all over the world came just to hear him drop knowledge, 'cause God had poured wisdom straight into his heart.
9.24: Every one of 'em brought gifts—gold, silver, clothes, armor, spices, horses, and mules. And they did it every year like clockwork.
9.25: Solomon had 4,000 stalls for horses and chariots, plus 12,000 horsemen spread across the chariot cities and Jerusalem.
9.26: He ruled over all the kings from the Euphrates River to the Philistine lands, all the way to Egypt's border.
9.27: In his time, silver was as common as rocks in Jerusalem, and cedar trees were everywhere like sycamores in the lowlands.
9.28: People brought him horses from Egypt and all over the world.
9.29: The rest of Solomon's story—from beginning to end—is written in the books by the prophets Nathan, Ahijah the Shilonite, and Iddo the seer, especially the stuff about Jeroboam.
9.30: Solomon reigned over all of Israel for 40 years, from Jerusalem.
9.31: Then he died and was buried in the City of David, right next to his father. And his son Rehoboam took the throne after him.

10.1: Rehoboam pulled up to Shechem, 'cause everybody in Israel had come through there to crown him king.
10.2: When Jeroboam, son of Nebat, heard what was goin' on—he was still chillin' in Egypt after runnin' from King Solomon—he came back.
10.3: The folks sent for him, and Jeroboam and the rest of Israel stepped to Rehoboam and said,
10.4: "Yo, your daddy worked us hard. That load was heavy. If you chill out and lighten up the workload he had on us, we'll ride with you."
10.5: Rehoboam was like, "Bet. Come back in three days and I'll tell y'all what's up." So they dipped.
10.6: Then the king went to the OGs, the elders that used to give Solomon advice, and asked, "What y'all think I should say to the people?"
10.7: They said, "If you treat these folks right, speak kindly, and show love, they'll rock with you forever."
10.8: But Rehoboam wasn't feelin' that. He tossed the elder advice and went to his homeboys—the ones he grew up with—and asked,
10.9: "What y'all think I should say to these folks askin' me to ease up on the load my dad put on 'em?"
10.10: His boys said, "Here's what you tell 'em: 'Y'all think my pops was tough? I'm worse! My pinky heavier than his whole waist!
10.11: My pops beat y'all with whips? I'm comin' with scorpions!'"
10.12: So Jeroboam and the people came back three days later, just like the king told 'em.
10.13: But Rehoboam came at 'em wild disrespectful. He didn't listen to the elders,
10.14: and instead he repeated what his crew told him: "My daddy made it hard? I'm makin' it harder. He beat y'all with whips? I got scorpions comin'!"
10.15: He ain't hear the people out, 'cause God had His hand in all this—He was settin' up what He already told Jeroboam through the prophet Ahijah from Shiloh.
10.16: When the people saw Rehoboam wasn't rockin' with them, they said, "We ain't got nothin' to do with David's house! Jesse's son ain't our people. Everybody go home! Take care of your own house, David!" So Israel bounced, each to their own.
10.17: But Rehoboam stayed king over the folks who were still livin' in Judah.
10.18: Then Rehoboam sent out Hadoram, the dude over taxes—but Israel wasn't havin' it. They stoned him till he died. Rehoboam had to hop in his chariot and get up outta there, back to Jerusalem.
10.19: And that's how the split happened—Israel been beefin' with the house of David ever since.

11.1: When Rehoboam got back to Jerusalem, he pulled together 180,000 soldiers from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin—his plan was to go to war with Israel and get the kingdom back under his rule.
11.2: But God sent a word to Shemaiah, the man of God, sayin',
11.3: "Tell Rehoboam, son of Solomon, king of Judah, and all the people from Judah and Benjamin this:
11.4: 'Don't go fightin' y'all own people. Don't go up against Israel. Everybody go back home, 'cause this situation came from Me.'" So they actually listened to the Lord and called off the attack on Jeroboam.
11.5: Rehoboam stayed in Jerusalem and started building up defense cities in Judah.
11.6: He built up Bethlehem, Etam, and Tekoa—
11.7: Also Beth Zur, Sochoh, and Adullam,
11.10: Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron—all of these were in Judah and Benjamin. Fortified and ready.
11.11: He made sure these strongholds had commanders, plus stashes of food, oil, and wine.
11.12: He stocked every city with shields and spears, beefed them up real strong, and had Judah and Benjamin riding with him.
11.13: All over Israel, the priests and Levites took their stand with Rehoboam.
11.14: The Levites left their hometowns and property behind to come to Judah and Jerusalem. Why? 'Cause Jeroboam and his sons had kicked them out the priesthood—they couldn't serve the Lord no more.
11.15: Jeroboam had set up his own priests for the high places, for fake gods, and them golden calf idols he made up.
11.16: So after the Levites dipped, folks from all over Israel who still had their heart set on the Lord packed up and moved to Jerusalem too. They came to worship the God of their ancestors and offer sacrifices in the right place.
11.17: That move strengthened Judah. Rehoboam held it down for three years straight, walking in the ways of David and Solomon—just like the old days.
11.18: Rehoboam married Mahalath—she was the daughter of Jerimoth (David's son) and Abihail (the daughter of Eliab, Jesse's son).
11.19: She gave him three sons: Jeush, Shamariah, and Zaham.
11.20: Then he married Maachah, Absalom's granddaughter. She gave him Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith.
11.21: Rehoboam was head over heels for Maachah—more than all his other wives and side chicks. Dude had 18 wives and 60 concubines, and he ended up with 28 sons and 60 daughters.
11.22: He picked Abijah, Maachah's son, to be the main one—the leader out of all his sons—'cause he planned to make him the next king.
11.23: Rehoboam played it smart—he spread his sons out across all the fortified cities in Judah and Benjamin, gave 'em plenty of supplies, and made sure they were good. Oh—and he made sure they had wives too. Rehoboam kept his family network deep.

12.1: So once Rehoboam got settled in as king and felt like he had it all under control, he stopped followin' God's law. And Israel followed his lead right into disobedience.
12.2: In the fifth year of Rehoboam's reign, Shishak—the king of Egypt—rolled up on Jerusalem, 'cause they had turned their backs on the Lord.
12.3: He wasn't playin' either—he brought 1,200 chariots, 60,000 horsemen, and a whole army too big to count. Folks came with him from Egypt, including the Lubim, Sukkiim, and Ethiopians.
12.4: Shishak took over all the fortified cities of Judah and pulled up right to Jerusalem.
12.5: That's when Shemaiah the prophet came to Rehoboam and the leaders of Judah, who were all holed up in Jerusalem. He said, "This what the Lord say: 'Y'all left Me, so now I'm lettin' you fall into Shishak's hands.'"
12.6: When the leaders and the king heard that, they humbled themselves and said, "The Lord is right. We messed up."
12.7: God saw that they were really humbling themselves, so He told Shemaiah, "Okay, since they came correct, I won't wipe them out. I'ma give 'em a little mercy. I won't let Shishak burn Jerusalem to the ground."
12.8: "But they still gon' serve him for a while—so they can learn the difference between servin' Me and servin' some regular king from these other nations."
12.9: So Shishak came and snatched up all the treasure from God's house and the king's palace—took everything. Even them gold shields Solomon had made? Gone.
12.10: So King Rehoboam had some bronze ones made instead and put 'em in the care of the guards who stood watch at the palace gates.
12.11: Every time Rehoboam went to the Lord's temple, the guards would bring the shields out, then put them back up when he left.
12.12: Because Rehoboam humbled himself, God didn't let everything fall apart. He pulled His anger back, and things in Judah stayed relatively stable.
12.13: Rehoboam stayed strong in Jerusalem and kept reignin'. He was 41 when he started, and he ruled for 17 years in Jerusalem—the same city God had picked to rep His name among all the tribes of Israel. His mama's name was Naamah, and she was from Ammon.
12.14: But Rehoboam still did wrong—'cause he never made it a priority to truly seek the Lord. His heart wasn't in it.
12.15: Everything else Rehoboam did—from start to finish—is written down in the records from Shemaiah the prophet and Iddo the seer, who also kept the family histories. And yeah—him and Jeroboam were beefin' the whole time.
12.16: Rehoboam eventually died and was buried in the City of David. His son Abijah took over the throne after him.

13.1: In the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam, Abijah stepped up as king of Judah.
13.2: He ruled for three years in Jerusalem. His mama's name was Michaiah, daughter of Uriel from Gibeah. There was serious beef between Abijah and Jeroboam.
13.3: Abijah got his army ready—400,000 top-tier soldiers, ready for war. Jeroboam pulled up too with double—800,000 strong, warriors ready to scrap.
13.4: Abijah stood on Mount Zemaraim, in the hill country of Ephraim, and shouted, "Aye! Jeroboam and all of Israel, listen up!"
13.5: "Y'all do remember that God gave the kingdom to David and his people forever, right? That covenant was sealed in salt—it's serious."
13.6: "But Jeroboam, son of Nebat, who used to serve Solomon (David's son), switched up and rebelled against the throne."
13.7: "Some low-down folks backed him up too. They came for Rehoboam when he was still young and green, and Rehoboam couldn't handle the pressure."
13.8: "Now y'all think you can stand against God's kingdom—the one He gave to David's crew? Just 'cause you deep in numbers and got them golden calves Jeroboam made for y'all to worship?"
13.9: "Didn't y'all kick out the Lord's real priests—Aaron's sons and the Levites? And then turned around and appointed your own priests like y'all were running some bootleg temple setup? Anyone with a young bull and seven rams could claim priesthood—even if they wasn't legit."
13.10: "But as for us—nah. We still rock with the Lord. We ain't left Him. Our priests are the real deal—Aaron's descendants. The Levites still doing what they supposed to."
13.11: "Every morning and night, they burn sacrifices and incense to the Lord. They keep the showbread in order on the gold table. They keep the lampstand lit every night. We follow what God told us to do. Y'all the ones who dipped out."
13.12: "Look—God Himself is with us. He's our leader. Our priests got the trumpets to sound off against y'all. So listen up, Israel—don't come fightin' against the Lord, the God of your ancestors. You ain't gon' win this."
13.13: Meanwhile, Jeroboam had already set up a sneak attack—an ambush behind Judah's forces. So they had enemies in front and behind.
13.14: When Judah turned around and saw they were boxed in, they cried out to the Lord. The priests blew the trumpets.
13.15: Judah let out a war cry—and when they did, God showed up and struck down Jeroboam's whole army. Judah came out on top.
13.16: Israel started running, and God handed them over to Judah.
13.17: Abijah and his crew laid 'em out—500,000 top soldiers from Israel died that day. Heavy losses.
13.18: Israel got humbled, and Judah came out victorious—'cause they leaned fully on the Lord, the God of their ancestors.
13.19: Abijah chased Jeroboam and took some cities: Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephrain—plus the surrounding areas.
13.20: Jeroboam never bounced back while Abijah was alive. God struck him down, and he died.
13.21: Abijah got stronger, married 14 wives, and had 22 sons and 16 daughters.
13.22: Everything else Abijah did—how he lived, what he said—is written down in the records from the prophet Iddo.

14.1: Abijah passed away and was buried in the City of David. His son Asa stepped up as king. During Asa's time, the land had peace for ten straight years.
14.2: Asa did what was right in God's eyes—he didn't play.
14.3: He tore down altars to foreign gods, shut down the high places, smashed the sacred pillars, and cut down the wooden idols.
14.4: He told everybody in Judah, "Y'all better seek the Lord—the God of our ancestors—and keep His laws straight up."
14.5: He even cleared out the incense altars and high places in every city across Judah. Because of that, the kingdom stayed calm and peaceful under his rule.
14.6: Asa built up fortified cities all through Judah. Since God had given him rest, there was no war goin' on during those years.
14.7: Asa said, "Let's go ahead and build up these cities now—put up walls, towers, gates, and bars—while things are still peaceful. We been seekin' the Lord, and He's holdin' us down on every side." So they built everything up and started to flourish.
14.8: Asa's army was tight: 300,000 from Judah, rockin' shields and spears, and 280,000 from Benjamin with shields and bows. All of 'em were solid warriors.
14.9: Then Zerah the Ethiopian showed up tryin' to test 'em—he brought a million soldiers and 300 chariots, posted up at Mareshah.
14.10: Asa rolled out to face him and lined up his troops in the Valley of Zephathah, right near Mareshah.
14.11: Asa cried out to God, "Lord, You don't need numbers to help—whether we got many or none, You got power. Help us, God! We're countin' on You, and we're fightin' this battle in Your name. Don't let these folks win against You!"
14.12: And just like that, the Lord struck down the Ethiopians right in front of Asa and Judah. They had to retreat.
14.13: Asa and his people chased them all the way to Gerar. The Ethiopians couldn't bounce back—they got crushed by the Lord and His army. Judah cleaned up and took a whole lotta loot.
14.14: They also took out the nearby towns around Gerar, 'cause everybody was shook—they feared the Lord heavy. Judah raided all the cities and left with a ton of goods.
14.15: Then they hit up the livestock pens and came back to Jerusalem loaded with sheep, camels, and all kinds of animals.

15.1: Then the Spirit of God came over Azariah, son of Oded.
15.2: He went to meet Asa and said, "Listen up, Asa—and everybody in Judah and Benjamin! The Lord is with y'all as long as y'all stay with Him. If you seek Him, you'll find Him. But if you walk away, He gon' do the same."
15.3: "For a long time, Israel didn't have the real God. No teaching priests, no law, just chaos."
15.4: "But when trouble hit and they turned back to the Lord God of Israel and looked for Him, He showed up."
15.5: "Back then, it was no peace—folks couldn't go in or out without drama. It was wild everywhere."
15.6: "Nations were crashin' into each other. Cities were fallin' apart. God let all kinds of struggle hit the land."
15.7: "But as for you—be strong, don't get tired. Keep pushin'. God sees you. Your work gon' get blessed."
15.8: When Asa heard that word from the prophet Oded, he got fired up. He went through Judah, Benjamin, and the cities he took in Ephraim, and wiped out all them nasty idols. Then he fixed the altar of the Lord that was in front of the temple entrance.
15.9: After that, he gathered everybody—Judah, Benjamin, and even folks from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon who had moved in. A bunch of people left Israel to join Asa when they saw God was ridin' with him.
15.10: They all came together in Jerusalem during the third month of Asa's fifteenth year on the throne.
15.11: And right then, they offered up 700 bulls and 7,000 sheep from the loot they had gotten in battle.
15.12: They made a covenant to seek the Lord—the God of their ancestors—with all their heart and soul.
15.13: And they were serious with it—anybody who didn't seek the Lord, no matter who they were, man or woman, rich or poor, was supposed to be put to death.
15.14: They shouted out their oath loud, with trumpets and rams' horns and all that.
15.15: All Judah was hyped—they made the vow with their whole heart, and they were serious about finding God. And He came through for them. God gave them peace all around.
15.16: Asa even had to check his own mama, Maachah. She had made a nasty image of the false goddess Asherah, so Asa stripped her of her title as queen mother. He chopped that idol down, crushed it to pieces, and burned it by the Kidron Brook.
15.17: The high places still weren't taken outta Israel, but Asa's heart was fully locked in with the Lord all his life.
15.18: He brought back all the silver, gold, and utensils that he and his father had dedicated, and put them in God's temple.
15.19: And there wasn't any war until Asa's thirty-fifth year as king.

16.1: In Asa's 36th year as king, Baasha—the king of Israel—came through and started buildin' up Ramah to block people from leavin' or comin' into Judah. He was tryna trap Asa in.
16.2: So Asa took silver and gold from the treasuries of both God's house and the royal palace, and sent it to Ben-Hadad, king of Syria, up in Damascus. He said,
16.3: "Let's make a deal—you and me—just like our daddies did. I'm sendin' you this silver and gold. Break that treaty you got with Baasha so he'll back off."
16.4: Ben-Hadad agreed. He sent his army commanders to hit Israel's cities. They attacked Ijon, Dan, Abel Maim, and all of Naphtali's supply cities.
16.5: When Baasha got wind of that, he stopped building Ramah and left the project undone.
16.6: Then Asa brought out the whole crew from Judah, and they grabbed all the stones and timber Baasha had stacked for Ramah. Asa reused that material to build up Geba and Mizpah.
16.7: Around that time, the seer Hanani came to King Asa and said, "You messed up. You leaned on Syria instead of leanin' on the Lord your God. Because of that, you missed out on takin' down Syria's army too."
16.8: "Remember the Ethiopians and the Lubim? They had a huge army with all them chariots and horsemen, but because you trusted God, He handed them to you."
16.9: "God's eyes are always movin'—lookin' across the whole earth to show up strong for the ones who really ride for Him. But you? You acted foolish. Now you're gonna have nothing but wars from here on out."
16.10: Asa didn't like that one bit. He got heated and locked Hanani up in prison. Dude was mad mad—and he started mistreatin' some of the people too.
16.11: Everything Asa did—beginning to end—is written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.
16.12: In his 39th year as king, Asa came down with a serious disease in his feet. It got real bad. But even then, he still didn't seek God—he just leaned on the doctors.
16.13: Asa died in his 41st year on the throne and was buried with his ancestors.
16.14: They laid him in the tomb he had prepared for himself in the City of David. His body was placed on a bed filled with spices and rich oils, and they lit a major fire in his honor—like a royal sendoff.

17.1: After Asa passed, his son Jehoshaphat took the throne. First thing he did was secure the kingdom—he built up defense against Israel.
17.2: He stationed troops in all the fortified cities of Judah, plus in the cities in Ephraim that his dad Asa had taken over.
17.3: God was with Jehoshaphat, no doubt. He walked like David used to—he wasn't out here chasing after the Baals.
17.4: Instead, he sought the God of his father and followed God's commandments—not Israel's ways.
17.5: Because of that, God made sure Jehoshaphat's rule was solid. Judah was behind him—they even brought him gifts. Bro was stackin' wealth and respect.
17.6: His heart was all in on following the Lord. He even went further—he tore down all the high places and wooden idols from Judah.
17.7: In year three of his reign, Jehoshaphat sent a crew of his top officials—Ben-Hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Michaiah—on a mission to teach in the cities of Judah.
17.8: With them he sent Levites—Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tobadonijah—plus two priests: Elishama and Jehoram.
17.9: They rolled through Judah with the Book of the Law and taught the people in every city. They made sure everybody knew God's Word.
17.10: And the fear of the Lord hit all the surrounding nations—nobody dared start mess with Jehoshaphat.
17.11: Even the Philistines brought him gifts and tribute silver. The Arabians pulled up too—with 7,700 rams and 7,700 male goats.
17.12: Jehoshaphat just kept gettin' stronger. He built fortresses and storage cities all over Judah.
17.13: He had a ton of property in the cities, and his military game was tight—his mighty men of war were based in Jerusalem.
17.14: Here's the breakdown of his army by family line: From Judah: Adnah led 300,000 elite soldiers.
17.16: Then Amasiah, son of Zichri—he volunteered outta love for the Lord—and had 200,000 strong warriors.
17.17: From Benjamin: Eliada, a beast in battle, led 200,000 armed with bows and shields.
17.18: Right next to him was Jehozabad, with 180,000 soldiers ready for war.
17.19: These were Jehoshaphat's personal army—outside of the troops he had posted in the fortified cities across Judah.

18.1: Jehoshaphat had money and respect—he was set. And through marriage, he got tied up with Ahab.
18.2: Some years later, he went down to visit Ahab in Samaria. Ahab threw a big cookout—oxen, sheep, all that—for Jehoshaphat and his crew, and started talkin' him into goin' to war at Ramoth Gilead.
18.3: Ahab, king of Israel, asked Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, "You ridin' with me to take back Ramoth Gilead?" Jehoshaphat said, "I'm with you. My people, your people. We in this together."
18.4: But Jehoshaphat added, "Let's check in with the Lord first though."
18.5: So Ahab gathered 400 prophets and asked, "Should we go to war at Ramoth Gilead or fall back?" They all said, "Go ahead, king! God's got you—you'll win."
18.6: But Jehoshaphat wasn't fully convinced. "Ain't there a real prophet of the Lord around here we can ask?"
18.7: Ahab said, "Yeah, there's one—Micaiah, son of Imla. But I can't stand him. He never says anything good about me—always bad." Jehoshaphat said, "Come on, king, don't say that."
18.8: So Ahab called one of his officers and said, "Go get Micaiah, quick."
18.9: The two kings—Ahab and Jehoshaphat—sat on their thrones in full royal gear, out by the gate of Samaria, while all the other prophets gave their big speeches.
18.10: Zedekiah, son of Chenaanah, even made iron horns and said, "This what the Lord says: 'With these, you'll smash the Syrians till they're gone!'"
18.11: All the prophets echoed that same message: "Go up, king! You got this. The Lord is handin' it over to you."
18.12: The messenger who went to get Micaiah pulled him aside and said, "Look, all the other prophets already hyped the king up. Just say the same thing, aight? Keep it positive."
18.13: Micaiah said, "Nah, I'ma say whatever the Lord tells me—nothing more, nothing less."
18.14: So he pulled up, and the king asked, "Micaiah, should we go to Ramoth Gilead or not?" Micaiah said, "Yeah, go ahead—you'll win."
18.15: Ahab said, "Stop playin'. How many times I gotta tell you to speak straight in the Lord's name?"
18.16: Then Micaiah got real: "I saw Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd. And the Lord said, 'These folks got no leader. Send everybody home in peace.'"
18.17: Ahab turned to Jehoshaphat: "Didn't I tell you he only brings bad news?"
18.18: But Micaiah kept goin': "Here's the real word from the Lord: I saw God sittin' on His throne, surrounded by all of heaven."
18.19: "God said, 'Who's gonna trick Ahab into goin' up to Ramoth Gilead so he can fall there?' One spirit said this, another said that—"
18.20: "Then a spirit stepped up and said, 'I'll handle it.' God asked, 'How?'"
18.21: "The spirit said, 'I'll be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.' God said, 'Do it. You'll succeed.'"
18.22: "So that's what happened. The Lord let a lying spirit speak through these prophets—and He's already declared disaster for you."
18.23: Zedekiah stepped up and slapped Micaiah, talkin' slick: "So where'd the Spirit of the Lord go when He left me to talk to you?"
18.24: Micaiah said, "You'll find out the day you're hiding in a back room scared for your life."
18.25: Then Ahab said, "Lock him up! Send him back to Amon and Joash."
18.26: "Tell them: 'The king says put this man in prison and feed him scraps until I come back safely.'"
18.27: Micaiah fired back, "If you make it back alive, the Lord ain't speak through me. Y'all heard that!"
18.28: So Ahab and Jehoshaphat went on to Ramoth Gilead anyway.
18.29: Ahab told Jehoshaphat, "I'ma disguise myself for battle—you wear your royal robes." So Ahab went in incognito.
18.30: The king of Syria had told his chariot captains, "Don't fight anybody—just aim for the king of Israel."
18.31: So when the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat, they said, "That's him!" They moved in on him, but Jehoshaphat cried out—and the Lord stepped in. God pulled the enemy off him.
18.32: Once they realized he wasn't the king of Israel, they backed off.
18.33: Then some random soldier pulled back his bow, fired off a shot, and hit Ahab between the joints in his armor—pure chance, but right on target. Ahab told his chariot driver, "I'm hit—get me outta here."
18.34: The fight raged on all day. Ahab stayed propped up in his chariot, watchin' the Syrians—but by sunset, he was dead.

19.1: Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, made it back to his palace in Jerusalem safe and sound.
19.2: But Jehu, son of Hanani the seer, came out to meet him and said, "You really out here helping the wicked and loving those who hate the Lord? That's why God's wrath is on you.
19.3: But you got some good in you too—you took down them Asherah poles and set your heart on seeking God."
19.4: Jehoshaphat stayed in Jerusalem, but then went back out among the people from Beersheba to the hills of Ephraim, bringing them back to the Lord, the God of their ancestors.
19.5: He appointed judges throughout all the fortified cities in Judah, city by city.
19.6: He told the judges, "Watch yourselves when you judge—you ain't doing this for people, but for the Lord. He's right there with you when you make decisions.
19.7: So let the fear of the Lord be on you. Judge carefully, 'cause the Lord our God don't play favorites and don't take bribes."
19.8: In Jerusalem too, Jehoshaphat appointed some Levites, priests, and family heads of Israel to handle the Lord's law and settle disputes. They were based in Jerusalem.
19.9: He gave them these orders: "You gotta serve faithfully with complete loyalty to the Lord.
19.10: Whenever your people from the cities bring cases about bloodshed, about laws, commands, statutes, or regulations, you gotta warn them not to sin against the Lord. Otherwise, His anger will come down on you and your people. Do this, and you won't be guilty.
19.11: Look, Amariah the chief priest is over you in all matters of the Lord, and Zebadiah son of Ishmael, the leader of Judah, in all the king's matters. The Levites will serve as your officials. Handle your business with confidence. The Lord is with those who do right."

20.1: After all that, the folks from Moab, Ammon, and some others from Mount Seir rolled up to start war with Jehoshaphat.
20.2: Somebody ran up and told him, "Yo, a huge army comin' for you from across the sea—outta Syria. They already down at Hazazon Tamar (a.k.a. En Gedi)!"
20.3: Jehoshaphat got shook. But instead of panickin', he locked in on God and called a fast across all Judah.
20.4: So everybody in Judah came together to ask the Lord for help. People pulled up from all over the kingdom, tryin' to seek God.
20.5: Jehoshaphat stood in front of the people in the Lord's temple courtyard and prayed,
20.6: "Lord God of our ancestors—you run heaven and earth. Ain't nobody messin' with Your power."
20.7: "Ain't You the same God who cleared out this land for us, your people, and gave it to Abraham—Your friend—for keeps?"
20.8: "We live here now. We built a place for You to be worshiped.
20.9: And You said if disaster ever hit—war, judgment, disease, or famine—we could pull up to this place, call on You, and You'd hear us and save us."
20.10: "But now, look—Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir comin' for us. The same folks You told us not to touch when we left Egypt."
20.11: "Now they tryna throw us out the land You gave us."
20.12: "Lord, You gon' let that slide? We don't have the numbers or the strength to fight this. We don't even know what to do. But we lookin' straight at You."
20.13: Everybody stood there—men, women, kids—all of Judah, silent before the Lord.
20.14: Then the Spirit of the Lord hit Jahaziel—a Levite from Asaph's line—and he spoke up in the middle of the crowd.
20.15: "Listen up, Judah, Jerusalem, and you too, King Jehoshaphat! This is what God says: Don't trip about this big army. This fight ain't even yours—it's God's."
20.16: "Tomorrow, roll out to face them. You'll find them comin' up at the Ascent of Ziz, near the end of the valley before the Wilderness of Jeruel."
20.17: "But here's the twist—you won't even have to fight. Just show up, take your position, and watch God work. Don't be scared. God's right there with y'all."
20.18: Jehoshaphat hit the ground, face down. All the people bowed too, worshiping the Lord.
20.19: Then the Levites from the Kohath and Korah crews stood up and praised God loud—real loud.
20.20: Early the next morning, they headed out to the Wilderness of Tekoa. Jehoshaphat stopped and said, "Listen up, Judah and Jerusalem: Believe in the Lord your God and y'all will stand firm. Trust His prophets and y'all will win."
20.21: He picked out some folks to go ahead of the army and lead with praise. They were singin': "Praise the Lord, 'Cause His mercy never runs out!"
20.22: As soon as they started singin' and praisin', God set ambushes against Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir—and they got wrecked.
20.23: Moab and Ammon turned on Mount Seir, wiped them out, and then turned on each other. Total chaos.
20.24: By the time Judah reached the lookout over the desert, all they saw was dead bodies. Nobody made it out alive.
20.25: Jehoshaphat and his crew rolled through and took the loot—gold, clothes, jewelry—so much they couldn't carry it all. Took three days to scoop it up.
20.26: On the fourth day, they met up in the Valley of Berachah (which means "Blessing") and praised the Lord. The name stuck.
20.27: Then they marched back to Jerusalem—Jehoshaphat leadin'—happy, celebratin', 'cause the Lord had flipped the whole situation on their enemies.
20.28: They pulled up to Jerusalem with harps, lutes, and trumpets, headin' straight into the temple.
20.29: When the surrounding nations heard how the Lord Himself fought against Israel's enemies, everybody backed off.
20.30: Jehoshaphat's kingdom stayed chill after that—God gave him peace on all sides.
20.31: Jehoshaphat became king of Judah at 35 years old. He ruled in Jerusalem for 25 years. His mama's name was Azubah, daughter of Shilhi.
20.32: He followed his dad Asa's example and stayed solid in God's eyes.
20.33: But the high places still weren't taken down, and the people hadn't fully committed to God yet.
20.34: Everything else Jehoshaphat did—from start to finish—is written in the book of Jehu (Hanani's son), and it's mentioned in the book of the kings of Israel.
20.35: Later on, Jehoshaphat teamed up with Ahaziah, king of Israel—a dude who did wicked stuff.
20.36: They joined forces to build ships to go to Tarshish, out of Ezion Geber.
20.37: But Eliezer, son of Dodavah from Mareshah, dropped a prophecy: "Since you linked up with that fool Ahaziah, God ain't blessing this. He's shutting it down." And sure enough, the ships got wrecked and never made the trip.

21.1: Jehoshaphat passed away and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David. Then his son Jehoram took the throne.
21.2: Jehoram had a bunch of brothers—Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, Azaryahu, Michael, and Shephatiah—all sons of King Jehoshaphat.
21.3: Their father gave 'em gifts—silver, gold, and other valuables. He even gave them control of some fortified cities in Judah. But the crown? That went to Jehoram, since he was the oldest.
21.4: Once Jehoram had the kingdom locked down, he made a power move—and not in a good way. He killed all his brothers and even some other royal officials. Ruthless.
21.5: Jehoram was 32 when he became king, and he ruled for 8 years in Jerusalem.
21.6: But instead of following his pops or granddad Asa, Jehoram moved like the kings of Israel. Why? 'Cause he married Ahab's daughter. Dude did evil in God's eyes.
21.7: Even with all that, the Lord didn't wipe out David's family line—because of the promise He made to David to always keep a light burning through his descendants.
21.8: During Jehoram's time, Edom broke away from Judah and set up their own king.
21.9: Jehoram rolled out with his commanders and chariots, pulled a surprise night attack, and fought back the Edomites who had surrounded him.
21.10: But still, Edom stayed independent from Judah to this very day. Libnah also rebelled, 'cause Jehoram had turned his back on the God of his ancestors.
21.11: On top of that, Jehoram built up idol worship spots in the mountains of Judah. He led the people in straight-up spiritual adultery and got the whole kingdom caught up in sin.
21.12: Then Jehoram got a letter—from the prophet Elijah, no less. It said: "This what the Lord, God of your father David, has to say:
21.13: You ain't followin' the path of your pops Jehoshaphat or your granddad Asa. Instead, you actin' like the corrupt kings of Israel. You dragged Judah and Jerusalem into spiritual mess, just like Ahab's crew. And you even killed your own brothers—the ones who were better than you."
21.14: "So here's what's gonna happen: the Lord gon' strike your family—your kids, your wives, and everything you got.
21.15: And you? You gon' get hit with a disease so bad in your gut, your intestines gon' literally fall out. And it ain't gon' be quick—it's gon' drag on."
21.16: Then the Lord stirred up some enemies—the Philistines and the Arabians near the Ethiopians.
21.17: They came through Judah and raided the king's palace. Took all his valuables, his wives, and his sons. Only one son, Jehoahaz (the youngest), was left.
21.18: And just like Elijah said, the Lord hit Jehoram with an incurable disease in his intestines.
21.19: After two painful years, his insides literally came out. He died in agony. And the people? They didn't even light the traditional fire for him like they did for the kings before him.
21.20: Jehoram was 32 when he started. He ruled for 8 years. When he died, nobody mourned him. They buried him in the City of David—but not in the royal tombs.

22.1: After Jehoram died, the people in Jerusalem made his youngest son Ahaziah king. All his older brothers had been killed by raiders that rolled with the Arabians. So Ahaziah, son of Jehoram, stepped up as king of Judah.
22.2: Ahaziah was 42 years old when he became king, and he only reigned one year in Jerusalem. His mama was Athaliah, the granddaughter of Omri.
22.3: He followed the ways of Ahab's family, 'cause his mama had him out here wildin'—she pushed him to do evil.
22.4: So Ahaziah did wrong in God's eyes, just like Ahab's crew. After his father died, Ahab's people were his advisors, and they led him straight to destruction.
22.5: He took their advice and joined Ahab's son Jehoram (king of Israel) in a war against Hazael, king of Syria, at Ramoth Gilead. Jehoram got wounded in the battle.
22.6: He went back to Jezreel to heal from the injuries he got at Ramah. So Ahaziah went down to visit him in Jezreel, checkin' on him while he was recoverin'.
22.7: But God used that trip to set Ahaziah up for his downfall. While he was there, he ended up rollin' out with Jehoram to face Jehu—God's chosen one to wipe out Ahab's house.
22.8: When Jehu started bringin' judgment on Ahab's family, he found the princes of Judah and Ahaziah's nephews rollin' with him—and he took them out.
22.9: Then Jehu went lookin' for Ahaziah. He found him hidin' out in Samaria, brought him in, and had him killed. But they still gave him a proper burial, sayin', "He was the son of Jehoshaphat, who truly sought the Lord with all his heart." And just like that, Ahaziah's family had nobody left fit to run the kingdom.
22.10: When Athaliah—Ahaziah's mom—saw her son was dead, she went full savage. She ordered the execution of every royal heir in the house of Judah.
22.11: But Jehoshabeath, King Jehoram's daughter (and Ahaziah's sister), snuck Ahaziah's baby boy Joash outta there, away from the massacre. She hid him and his nurse in a bedroom. Jehoshabeath was married to Jehoiada the priest, and she kept Joash hidden from Athaliah.
22.12: Joash stayed hidden in God's temple with them for six whole years, while Athaliah ran the kingdom.

23.1: In the seventh year, Jehoiada (the priest) got bold. He made a pact with five military leaders—Azariah son of Jeroham, Ishmael son of Jehohanan, Azariah son of Obed, Maaseiah son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat son of Zichri.
23.2: They traveled all over Judah, got the Levites and tribal leaders on board, and brought everybody to Jerusalem.
23.3: In God's temple, they made a covenant with Joash, the young king. Jehoiada told them, "This right here is the king's son. He gon' reign just like the Lord said about David's bloodline."
23.4: "Here's the plan: A third of you Levites and priests will be on door duty on the Sabbath."
23.5: "Another third goes to guard the palace. And the last third will be at the Foundation Gate. Everybody else stays in the courtyards of the Lord's temple."
23.6: "Nobody steps inside the temple itself except the priests and Levites who are assigned. They the only ones allowed, 'cause they're holy. The rest of y'all stay posted outside."
23.7: "The Levites need to surround the king, armed up. If anyone tries to force their way in—drop 'em. Y'all protect the king when he moves in or out."
23.8: The Levites and the rest of Judah did exactly what Jehoiada said. The ones coming on duty that Sabbath linked up with the ones going off duty—nobody was dismissed.
23.9: Jehoiada handed out the weapons—spears and shields that used to belong to King David. They had been kept in the temple.
23.10: He had everyone posted with their weapons, standing from one end of the temple to the other, guarding the altar and the king.
23.11: Then they brought out Joash, the king's son. They crowned him, gave him the covenant scroll, anointed him, and everybody shouted, "Long live the king!"
23.12: Athaliah heard the noise—folks running, cheering—and she ran up to the Lord's temple to see what was goin' on.
23.13: She looked and saw Joash posted at the pillar like a real king. Leaders and trumpeters were with him. The crowd was hype, praising God with instruments. Athaliah tore her clothes and yelled, "Treason! Treason!"
23.14: Jehoiada called the army captains and told them, "Grab her. Don't kill her in here. If anybody tries to help her—cut 'em down."
23.15: They grabbed Athaliah, dragged her out through the Horse Gate entrance to the palace, and executed her right there.
23.16: Jehoiada then made a sacred agreement between himself, the people, and the king: they all belonged to the Lord now.
23.17: The whole crowd went straight to the temple of Baal and tore it to pieces. They smashed the altars, the idols, and killed Mattan the priest of Baal right there.
23.18: Jehoiada put the Lord's temple back in order. He put the Levite priests—just like David assigned—back in charge of offerings, music, and celebration, following Moses' law and David's blueprint.
23.19: He also assigned gatekeepers so nobody unclean could step inside the temple.
23.20: Then Jehoiada and the leaders brought Joash from the temple to the royal palace. They walked him through the Upper Gate and sat him down on the throne like a real king.
23.21: The people were rejoicing. The whole city calmed down. Athaliah was gone—killed by the sword.

24.1: Joash was only seven years old when he became king, and he ruled for forty years in Jerusalem. His mama's name was Zibiah from Beersheba.
24.2: Joash did right by God—for as long as Jehoiada the priest was alive.
24.3: Jehoiada hooked him up with two wives, and Joash had sons and daughters.
24.4: After a while, Joash made up his mind to fix up the temple of the Lord.
24.5: He called the priests and Levites together and said, "Y'all need to go collect money from across Judah and Israel every year to repair God's house. And don't drag your feet."
24.6: But the Levites were slow with it. So the king called in Jehoiada and asked, "Why haven't you made sure they're collecting the offering Moses commanded? That money's for God's house, not to sit around."
24.7: See, Athaliah's sons—yeah, that evil queen—had broken into the temple and taken the sacred stuff to use for Baal worship.
24.8: So the king ordered them to build a big chest and put it outside near the temple gate.
24.9: Then they sent word throughout Judah and Jerusalem, reminding everyone to bring their offering to the Lord—just like Moses said back in the wilderness days.
24.10: The leaders and the people were hyped—they gave joyfully and kept filling up the chest.
24.11: Whenever the chest filled up, the king's officials and the high priest's crew would empty it, then put it back. They kept that routine going day after day. Money was coming in heavy.
24.12: Joash and Jehoiada used the funds to hire workers—masons, carpenters, metalworkers—who put in the work to restore the temple.
24.13: The crew stayed at it till the job was done. God's house was back to how it used to be—and stronger.
24.14: With the extra money, they made gold and silver tools for offerings and temple service. Burnt offerings were back in full effect as long as Jehoiada lived.
24.15: Jehoiada lived a long, full life—130 years—and then he passed.
24.16: They buried him in the City of David with the kings 'cause he had done so much good for God and the people.
24.17: After Jehoiada died, the leaders of Judah came bowin' down to Joash—and he listened to them.
24.18: Just like that, they left the Lord's temple and started servin' idols and statues again. God's anger came down on Judah and Jerusalem for fallin' off so hard.
24.19: God sent prophets to warn 'em, tryin' to get them back on track. But they ignored every warning.
24.20: Then the Spirit of God came over Zechariah, Jehoiada's son. He stood in front of the people and said, "This is what God says: Why y'all breakin' God's commandments? That's why y'all not prosperin'. You abandoned God, so now He's leavin' y'all."
24.21: Instead of repentin', they plotted on him. And by Joash's own order, they stoned Zechariah right there in the temple courtyard.
24.22: Joash forgot all about the loyalty and kindness Jehoiada had shown him. He let his son get murdered. Zechariah's last words were, "Lord, don't let this slide. Handle this."
24.23: That spring, Syria came rollin' through. They attacked Judah and Jerusalem, wiped out the leaders, and sent all the loot back to their king in Damascus.
24.24: Crazy part? The Syrians weren't even deep like that—it was a small army. But God handed over Judah 'cause they had turned their backs on Him. Judgment hit Joash hard.
24.25: After the Syrians left Joash badly wounded, his own servants turned on him. They killed him in his bed—because of what he did to Zechariah, Jehoiada's son. They buried him in the City of David—but not in the royal tombs.
24.26: The ones who set him up were Zabad (whose mama was an Ammonite) and Jehozabad (whose mama was a Moabite).
24.27: You can read more about Joash—his sons, the prophecies about him, and the temple repairs—in the Book of the Kings. After he died, his son Amaziah took over the throne.

25.1: Amaziah was 25 when he became king, and he ruled for 29 years in Jerusalem. His mama was Jehoaddan from Jerusalem.
25.2: He did what was right in God's eyes—but his heart wasn't all the way in it.
25.3: As soon as he got settled as king, he executed the servants who had murdered his dad.
25.4: But he didn't kill their kids. He followed what Moses wrote in God's law: "Parents don't die for their kids' sins, and kids don't die for their parents' sins—everybody answers for their own."
25.5: Amaziah gathered Judah's army, broke them into units—captains of thousands and hundreds—and counted everybody 20 and up. He had 300,000 skilled warriors, ready with shields and spears.
25.6: Then he hired 100,000 extra soldiers from Israel for 100 talents of silver.
25.7: But a man of God came and said, "King, don't bring Israel's army with you. The Lord ain't with them—especially not with the tribe of Ephraim.
25.8: You roll with them anyway, you gon' lose. God's got the power to lift you up or shut you down."
25.9: Amaziah said, "But what about the money I already dropped on them?" The man of God said, "God can give you way more than that."
25.10: So Amaziah let the Israelite soldiers go home. They were heated—left Judah mad as ever.
25.11: Amaziah led his army to the Valley of Salt and killed 10,000 people from Seir.
25.12: Then they took another 10,000 alive, marched them to the top of a cliff, and tossed them off—brutal.
25.13: Meanwhile, those Israelite soldiers he sent home? They raided towns from Samaria to Beth Horon, killed 3,000 people, and took everything they could carry.
25.14: After that big W over Edom, Amaziah made a wild move—he brought back Edom's gods, set them up, and started worshipin' them.
25.15: God was furious. He sent a prophet who said, "Why you worshipin' gods who couldn't even save their own people from you?"
25.16: Amaziah cut him off: "Who asked you? You tryin' to be my advisor now? Watch yourself before you get killed." The prophet backed off and said, "I see where this is goin'. God's already decided—He's gonna let you fall 'cause you won't listen."
25.17: Amaziah ignored the warning and sent a challenge to Joash, king of Israel: "Let's square up."
25.18: Joash hit back with a parable: "A little weed in Lebanon told a cedar tree, 'Let me marry your daughter.' But a wild animal walked by and crushed it.
25.19: Basically—you beat Edom and now you gassed. Sit down before you get dragged—and Judah with you."
25.20: But Amaziah wouldn't listen. God let him charge into a loss 'cause of them false gods he bowed to.
25.21: So Joash of Israel and Amaziah of Judah met in battle at Beth Shemesh, in Judah's territory.
25.22: Judah lost bad. Everybody scattered and ran back to their tents.
25.23: Joash caught Amaziah at Beth Shemesh, brought him to Jerusalem, and knocked down 400 cubits of the city wall—from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate.
25.24: Then he raided the temple and palace—took the gold, silver, and whatever treasures were there. He even took hostages before heading back to Samaria.
25.25: Amaziah outlived Joash of Israel by 15 years.
25.26: Everything else he did is written in the records of Judah's and Israel's kings.
25.27: But after Amaziah turned his back on God, folks plotted on him. He ran to Lachish, but they tracked him down and killed him there.
25.28: They brought his body back on horses and buried him with his ancestors in the City of Judah.

26.1: After Amaziah died, everybody in Judah crowned his 16-year-old son Uzziah as king.
26.2: One of his first moves was rebuilding Elath and bringing it back under Judah's control.
26.3: Uzziah was just 16 when he became king, and he ruled for 52 years in Jerusalem. His mama was Jecholiah from Jerusalem.
26.4: He did right by God, just like his daddy Amaziah had done.
26.5: Uzziah was serious about seekin' God, especially while Zechariah the prophet was around to guide him with divine insight. As long as he kept seeking the Lord, God kept blessing him.
26.6: Uzziah went to war against the Philistines. He tore down the walls of Gath, Jabneh, and Ashdod, then built up cities around there to lock it down.
26.7: God had his back—whether it was against the Philistines, the Arabians in Gur Baal, or the Meunites.
26.8: Even the Ammonites were bringin' him tribute. Word about Uzziah spread all the way to Egypt. Dude was strong and well-respected.
26.9: He built towers at key spots around Jerusalem—Corner Gate, Valley Gate, and the angle of the wall—and fortified them.
26.10: He built towers in the desert too, dug out a bunch of wells. Uzziah had livestock everywhere, from the lowlands to the hills. He had vineyards and farms, because he loved working the land.
26.11: Uzziah also had a well-organized army. Jeiel the scribe and Maaseiah the officer kept the records under Captain Hananiah.
26.13: Over a massive army—307,500 warriors—ready to go to war and protect the king.
26.14: Uzziah made sure they were stacked—shields, spears, helmets, body armor, bows, and even slings for hurlin' stones.
26.15: He even had engineers invent war machines to mount on towers and corners to launch arrows and big rocks. His fame blew up. He was blessed and backed up—until he got too full of himself.
26.16: Once Uzziah got strong, his pride went to his head. That's when it all started goin' downhill. He walked up in the temple and tried to burn incense at the altar—something only priests were allowed to do.
26.17: Azariah the priest and 80 other bold priests ran up in there and confronted him.
26.18: They told him straight up: "Uzziah, this ain't your lane. Only the priests—Aaron's line—are consecrated to do this. You crossed a line. Get out! You not gon' get no honor from God for this."
26.19: But Uzziah got mad. He was holdin' the incense burner, ready to pop off—but right then, leprosy broke out on his forehead right in front of everybody.
26.20: When the priests saw it, they rushed him out—and he didn't argue. He knew God had struck him.
26.21: From then on, Uzziah lived with leprosy until he died. He had to stay isolated, couldn't even go to the temple no more. His son Jotham had to take over royal duties and judge the people.
26.22: The rest of Uzziah's story—from start to finish—was recorded by the prophet Isaiah, son of Amoz.
26.23: When Uzziah died, they buried him in the royal field (not the main tombs), because folks said, "That's the king who had leprosy." And his son Jotham took the throne after him.

27.1: Jotham was 25 when he became king, and he ruled for 16 years in Jerusalem. His mama's name was Jerushah, daughter of Zadok.
27.2: He did right in God's eyes—just like his father Uzziah. But unlike his pops, he didn't overstep by trying to enter the temple. Still, the people around him kept actin' shady.
27.3: Jotham rebuilt the Upper Gate of the Lord's temple, and he put in serious work strengthening the wall of Ophel.
27.4: He also built towns in the hill country of Judah, plus fortresses and watchtowers out in the forest areas.
27.5: He went to war with the king of the Ammonites and beat him. That year, the Ammonites paid up: 100 talents of silver, 10,000 kors of wheat, and 10,000 of barley. They kept sending that tribute in the second and third years too.
27.6: Jotham got stronger and stronger—because he stayed ready and steady in the Lord. He made sure his steps lined up with God's path.
27.7: Everything else he did—his battles, his leadership style—it's all written down in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah.
27.8: He was 25 when he started and ruled 16 years in Jerusalem.
27.9: Then Jotham passed, was buried in the City of David with his ancestors, and his son Ahaz became king next.

28.1: Ahaz was 20 when he became king, and he ruled for 16 years in Jerusalem. But he didn't walk right like David—he did not do what was right in God's eyes.
28.2: He followed the same reckless ways as the kings of Israel and made idols for the Baals.
28.3: He went as far as burnin' incense in the Valley of Hinnom and even sacrificed his own kids in fire—just like the wild nations God had already wiped out.
28.4: He worshiped on every hill and under every shady tree, burnin' incense wherever he could.
28.5: So God handed Ahaz over to the king of Syria. They beat him down and took a bunch of his people back to Damascus. Then Israel came through and wrecked shop too—huge slaughter.
28.6: Pekah (Remaliah's son) killed 120,000 warriors in one day—all because Judah had turned away from God.
28.7: One of Ephraim's soldiers, Zichri, killed the king's son Maaseiah, the palace manager Azrikam, and Elkanah, who was basically the king's right-hand man.
28.8: Then Israel snatched up 200,000 people—women, sons, and daughters—and took a ton of stuff from Judah, heading back to Samaria.
28.9: But there was a prophet of the Lord in Samaria named Oded. He stepped out to meet the returning army and said, "Look, God let y'all win 'cause He was mad at Judah—but y'all took it too far. That rage hit heaven."
28.10: "And now you wanna make your own people slaves? You just as guilty!"
