28.11: "Listen up—let those folks go back home, or God's wrath gonna land on y'all heavy."
28.12: A few Ephraimite leaders—Azariah, Berechiah, Jehizkiah, and Amasa—stood up and backed Oded.
28.13: They told the army, "Nah, we can't bring these captives here. We already in trouble with God—you tryna add fuel to the fire?"
28.14: So the soldiers gave up the captives and the loot right in front of the leaders and the crowd.
28.15: Then the leaders who were named helped out—clothed the naked, gave 'em shoes, food, water, even some oil. They put the weak ones on donkeys, and everyone got escorted back to Jericho, the City of Palms. Then the army went back to Samaria.
28.16: Around that same time, Ahaz begged Assyria for help.
28.17: Meanwhile, Edom rolled through and snatched some folks from Judah.
28.18: The Philistines invaded the lowlands and southern cities—Beth Shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, Sochoh, Timnah, Gimzo—they took it all.
28.19: Judah was fallin' apart, and God let it happen—'cause Ahaz had turned the people wild and kept dissin' the Lord.
28.20: So when Tiglath-Pileser, king of Assyria, showed up, he didn't help Ahaz at all—he stressed him even more.
28.21: Ahaz tried to pay him off with treasures from God's temple, the palace, and his officials. But it didn't work.
28.22: Even in his worst moment, Ahaz didn't get right with God—he got worse.
28.23: He started worshipin' the gods of Damascus—the same gods that just beat him. He thought, "They help Syria, maybe they'll help me." But they only led him and his people to ruin.
28.24: He stripped down the Lord's temple, broke the holy items, locked the temple doors, and built altars on every corner in Jerusalem.
28.25: In every city of Judah, he built high places to burn incense to fake gods. He made God furious.
28.26: Everything else he did—from start to finish—is written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.
28.27: When Ahaz died, they buried him in Jerusalem—but not in the royal tombs. His son Hezekiah took the throne after him.

29.1: Hezekiah was 25 when he took the throne, and he ruled for 29 years in Jerusalem. His mama was Abijah, daughter of Zechariah.
29.2: He did right in the eyes of the Lord—just like his ancestor David used to.
29.3: First year, first month of his reign, Hezekiah opened up the doors of the temple and fixed them.
29.4: Then he gathered the priests and Levites and brought them to the East Square.
29.5: He told them, "Listen up, y'all. Get yourselves right. Get this temple right. Clean out all the junk that's piled up in God's house."
29.6: "Our ancestors straight-up abandoned the Lord. Turned their backs on Him. Shut the doors, blew out the lamps, quit burning incense, stopped making offerings—like they just walked away from everything."
29.7: "That's why the Lord's anger hit Judah and Jerusalem so hard. That's why we've been mocked, attacked, and dragged into exile."
29.8: "Look around—our people, our families—we've been takin' losses."
29.9: "But now I'm ready to make a covenant with the Lord, so His anger can turn away from us."
29.10: "My sons, don't slack off now. The Lord picked y'all to stand in front of Him, serve Him, and keep the incense burning."
29.11: Then the Levites rose up: Mahath and Joel from the Kohathites; Kish and Azariah from the Merarites; Joah and Eden from the Gershonites;
29.12: Shimri and Jeiel from Elizaphan's family; Zechariah and Mattaniah from Asaph's line;
29.13: Jehiel and Shimei from Heman's crew; Shemaiah and Uzziel from Jeduthun's line.
29.14: They called their people together, purified themselves, and went to clean out the Lord's temple just like Hezekiah said.
29.15: The priests went deep inside the temple, gathered up all the filth and trash, brought it out to the courtyard, and the Levites took it all to the Brook Kidron.
29.16: They started purifying the temple on the first day of the first month. By the eighth day they hit the outer area. It took eight more days to finish everything. By the sixteenth day, it was done.
29.17: Then they came back to Hezekiah and said, "We cleaned it all—the temple, the altar, the table of showbread, and all the items.
29.18: We even restored the stuff Ahaz trashed during his reign. It's all been purified and set up at the altar now."
29.19: "Also, all the stuff King Ahaz threw out back when he was wildin'? We got it all cleaned up and ready again. Everything's been purified and now it's sittin' right there in front of the Lord's altar."
29.20: Early the next morning, Hezekiah gathered the city officials and headed to the temple.
29.21: They brought seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven goats as a sin offering—for the nation, the temple, and all of Judah. He told the priests to offer them to the Lord.
29.22: They killed the bulls, the priests took the blood and sprinkled it on the altar. Same with the rams. Same with the lambs.
29.23: Then they brought the goats for the sin offering, laid hands on them—symbolic transfer of sin.
29.24: The priests killed the goats, sprinkled the blood on the altar to make atonement for all Israel—because Hezekiah said, "This offering ain't just for Judah—it's for the whole people."
29.25: Then he posted up the Levites in the temple with cymbals, harps, and stringed instruments—just like David, Gad the prophet, and Nathan had ordered based on God's command.
29.26: The Levites got on the instruments, and the priests stood ready with the trumpets.
29.27: When the burnt offering started, the worship started. Trumpets blasted. Songs played. All of it was for the Lord.
29.28: The crowd worshiped, singers sang, trumpeters blew—it kept goin' until the offering was done.
29.29: When it ended, the king and everybody bowed down and worshiped.
29.30: Hezekiah and the leaders told the Levites to sing songs from David and Asaph. They sang with joy and bowed their heads low in reverence.
29.31: Hezekiah said, "Now that y'all've rededicated yourselves, bring your sacrifices and thank offerings." So the people pulled up with everything—they brought what was on their hearts to give.
29.32: The numbers? 70 bulls, 100 rams, 200 lambs—all for burnt offerings.
29.33: Plus 600 bulls and 3,000 sheep for consecration.
29.34: There weren't enough priests to handle it all, so the Levites—who were more on point—jumped in to help until the rest of the priests got sanctified.
29.35: There were so many offerings—burnt, peace, drink offerings—the temple was full and active again.
29.36: Hezekiah and the people were rejoicing. God had moved the people's hearts fast—it all came together quicker than anyone expected.

30.1: Hezekiah sent word to all of Israel and Judah—he even wrote letters to Ephraim and Manasseh—inviting everybody to come to the Lord's house in Jerusalem and keep the Passover to the God of Israel.
30.2: The king, his leaders, and the whole assembly had agreed to push Passover to the second month.
30.3: They couldn't keep it at the regular time 'cause not enough priests had gotten themselves ready, and the people hadn't gathered yet.
30.4: But the plan sounded good to the king and everybody else.
30.5: So they sent out a call from Beersheba to Dan—"Y'all come to Jerusalem and celebrate Passover like we're supposed to. It's been way too long since it was done right."
30.6: Messengers ran across the land with the king's letter. It said, "Israel—come back to the Lord, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. If you return, He'll receive those of you who escaped Assyria's grip."
30.7: "Don't be like your fathers and relatives who disrespected God. Look where that got them—ruined."
30.8: "Don't be stubborn like they were. Surrender to the Lord. Come back into His sanctuary, the one He set apart forever. Serve Him, and maybe He'll turn His anger away."
30.9: "If y'all come back to the Lord, He'll show mercy to your families, even the ones in captivity. He's full of grace—if you reach for Him, He won't turn His back."
30.10: The runners went through Ephraim, Manasseh, all the way to Zebulun—but a lotta folks just laughed and clowned them.
30.11: Still, some people from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and made their way to Jerusalem.
30.12: Meanwhile, God worked on Judah's heart, giving them unity to follow the king's word and the Lord's command.
30.13: A massive crowd gathered in Jerusalem for the Feast of Unleavened Bread in the second month.
30.14: First thing they did? Tore down every altar they could find in the city—smashed the incense spots and dumped it all in the Brook Kidron.
30.15: Then they killed the Passover lambs on the 14th day of the second month. The priests and Levites felt convicted, got themselves right, and brought burnt offerings to the temple.
30.16: The priests took their spots like Moses had instructed, and the Levites handed them the blood to sprinkle on the altar.
30.17: A lot of the people weren't ritually clean, so the Levites had to step in and handle the lambs on their behalf.
30.18: Folks from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun hadn't purified themselves properly, but they still showed up to seek God and eat the Passover.
30.19: Hezekiah prayed, "Lord, forgive everyone who came with a sincere heart—even if they ain't fully clean."
30.20: And God heard that prayer—and healed the people.
30.21: Everybody kept the feast for seven days, full of joy. The Levites and priests praised the Lord daily, singing loud with instruments.
30.22: Hezekiah spoke life into the Levites who were teachin' God's Word, and they all ate together, offered peace offerings, and confessed their sins out loud to the God of their ancestors.
30.23: Then the people said, "Let's run it back!" They kept the feast for another seven days—with even more joy.
30.24: Hezekiah gave the crowd 1,000 bulls and 7,000 sheep. The leaders added 1,000 bulls and 10,000 sheep. A whole crew of priests purified themselves and joined in.
30.25: The entire crew—Judah, the priests, the Levites, Israelites from outta town, foreigners living in Judah—everybody was rejoicing together.
30.26: There hadn't been a celebration like that in Jerusalem since Solomon, son of David, was king. This was historic joy.
30.27: The priests and Levites stood up and blessed the people. Their voices were heard. Their prayers went straight to heaven—God's holy place.

31.1: After all that worship and celebration, everybody who came out from Israel went back to their towns—but not before they smashed every idol and altar they could find. From Judah and Benjamin to Ephraim and Manasseh, they tore down sacred pillars, chopped down wooden images, and wrecked the high places. Once the cleanup was done, everybody headed home.
31.2: Hezekiah set up the priest and Levite crews again, assigning them by their divisions—each one with specific roles: burn offerings, peace offerings, praise, and thanksgiving at the gates of the temple.
31.3: The king also gave from his own stash for the daily sacrifices—morning and evening—and for the Sabbaths, new moons, and other feast days, just like it says in the Law of the Lord.
31.4: He told the folks in Jerusalem to make sure the priests and Levites were taken care of, so they could focus fully on God's law.
31.5: As soon as the word spread, the people responded. They started bringing firstfruits—grain, wine, oil, honey, everything they harvested—and they gave tithes off it all.
31.6: Folks from both Israel and Judah, wherever they lived, brought in their tithes of oxen, sheep, and everything else they had dedicated to God. It was so much, it stacked up in heaps.
31.7: They started bringing it in around the third month, and by the seventh month, they were still piling it up.
31.8: When Hezekiah and the leaders saw all the stacks, they praised God and blessed the people.
31.9: Hezekiah asked the priests and Levites, "What's up with all these heaps?"
31.10: Azariah the high priest (from Zadok's line) told him, "Ever since the people started giving, we've had more than enough to eat—and this overflow? That's just the extra. The Lord really blessed His people."
31.11: So Hezekiah had them build storage rooms in the temple, and they got it done.
31.12: The people faithfully brought in their offerings, tithes, and dedicated items. Cononiah the Levite was in charge, with his brother Shimei as his right hand.
31.13: Under them were a crew of faithful managers: Jehiel, Azaziah, Nahath, Asahel, Jerimoth, Jozabad, Eliel, Ismachiah, Mahath, and Benaiah. All of them followed Hezekiah's and Azariah's orders.
31.14: Kore (son of Imnah the Levite) was the gatekeeper on the east side. He was in charge of the freewill offerings, and made sure everything got distributed properly.
31.15: Under him were Eden, Miniamin, Jeshua, Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah—faithful workers in the priestly towns. They handed out shares to all the priests, no matter their rank.
31.16: They gave out daily portions to every male from age 3 and up who was registered to serve in the Lord's house,
31.17: including all the priests and Levites, based on their divisions and duties, from age 20 and up.
31.18: Everyone in the records—their kids, wives, sons, and daughters—got taken care of too, because they had been faithful and set apart for God.
31.19: Even in the priestly towns out in the countryside, there were men assigned by name to make sure every male Levite and priest got what they were due.
31.20: Hezekiah held it down all over Judah. He stayed true to what was good, right, and real in God's eyes.
31.21: Everything he did—whether in the temple, the law, or keeping God's commands—he did it with his whole heart. That's why he prospered.

32.1: After Hezekiah did all that right and faithful stuff, Sennacherib, king of Assyria, came for Judah. He set up camp outside the fortified cities, tryin' to snatch them for himself.
32.2: When Hezekiah saw Sennacherib's army posted up with plans to attack Jerusalem,
32.3: he met with his leaders and commanders and said, "Let's cut off all the water sources outside the city." And they helped him make it happen.
32.4: A whole crew came together and stopped up the springs and the stream that ran through the land. They said, "Why should the king of Assyria roll up and find plenty of water?"
32.5: Hezekiah got to work—he rebuilt the broken parts of the wall, built towers, added another outer wall, repaired the Millo in the City of David, and stocked up on weapons and shields.
32.6: Then he appointed captains over the people, gathered everybody in the city square, and told them,
32.7: "Be strong and brave! Don't trip over the king of Assyria or his whole army. We got more on our side than he got on his."
32.8: "He rollin' with human power—but we got the Lord our God with us. He's fightin' our battles." The people felt fired up after Hezekiah's words.
32.9: While Sennacherib was still busy takin' Lachish, he sent messengers to Hezekiah and everybody in Jerusalem.
32.10: They said, "What y'all think y'all doin' stayin' locked up in Jerusalem? Y'all really trust Hezekiah when he says, 'The Lord will deliver us'?"
32.11: "You gon' sit there hungry and thirsty waitin' on this so-called rescue? Hezekiah's got y'all fooled."
32.12: "Didn't that same Hezekiah tear down the high places and altars, and say y'all could only worship at one altar?"
32.13: "Y'all must not know what me and my people did to all the other nations. Their gods couldn't save them from me—
32.14: what makes you think your God gon' do any better?"
32.15: "Don't let Hezekiah gas you. No god has been able to stop me yet—and your God ain't gon' be the first."
32.16: His crew kept trash talkin' the Lord and dissin' Hezekiah too.
32.17: Sennacherib even wrote letters talkin' reckless: "Your God can't save you no more than all them other gods saved their people."
32.18: Then they shouted threats in Hebrew at the folks on the wall—tryin' to scare them into givin' up.
32.19: They talked about the God of Jerusalem like He was just another fake idol made by human hands.
32.20: Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah cried out to God in prayer.
32.21: And the Lord answered—He sent an angel who wiped out every strong warrior, commander, and officer in the Assyrian army. Sennacherib had to pack up and head home ashamed. And when he got back to his temple, some of his own sons killed him right there.
32.22: So the Lord saved Hezekiah and Jerusalem from Sennacherib and anyone else who tried them. God had their back on all sides.
32.23: Folks from everywhere brought gifts to God in Jerusalem and gifts to King Hezekiah. After that, he was respected by all the nations.
32.24: Later, Hezekiah got sick—real close to death. He prayed, and God spoke to him and gave him a sign.
32.25: But Hezekiah didn't give God the praise He deserved. Pride crept in, and wrath started buildin' over Judah and Jerusalem.
32.26: But then Hezekiah and the people humbled themselves, and the Lord's judgment didn't fall during his time.
32.27: Hezekiah had wealth and honor stacked up. He built treasuries for gold, silver, gems, spices, shields—everything valuable.
32.28: He built storehouses for crops, wine, and oil, and barns for livestock and flocks.
32.29: He even built himself some cities. Dude had property everywhere. God really blessed him.
32.30: He also re-routed water from the Upper Gihon spring through a tunnel into Jerusalem. Hezekiah stayed winnin'.
32.31: But when Babylon sent messengers to check out the miracle that happened in the land, God pulled back for a moment—to test Hezekiah's heart and see what was really inside.
32.32: Everything else Hezekiah did—his faith, his record—it's all written in Isaiah's visions and in the kings' chronicles.
32.33: When he died, they buried him in the royal tombs with David's descendants. All of Judah and Jerusalem showed him love when he passed. Then his son Manasseh became king.

33.1: Manasseh was just 12 when he became king, and he ruled for 55 years in Jerusalem.
33.2: But he was wild—he did evil in the Lord's eyes, copying the same nasty stuff the nations before Israel were doing.
33.3: He brought back the high places his father Hezekiah had torn down, built altars for Baal, made Asherah poles, and worshiped the stars and planets.
33.4: Dude even built altars inside the Lord's temple—the very place God said, "My name gon' stay in Jerusalem forever."
33.5: He set up altars to the stars in both temple courtyards.
33.6: He burned his own sons in fire in the Valley of Hinnom. He was deep in sorcery, witchcraft, mediums, and talking to spirits—straight evil, and God was not pleased.
33.7: He even put an idol he made inside God's temple—the same temple where God told David and Solomon, "This is My spot. My name stays here forever if y'all obey Me."
33.8: God said He'd keep Israel planted in their land if they stuck to His laws—but Manasseh led Judah to wild out harder than the nations God had already destroyed.
33.9: Manasseh dragged Judah and Jerusalem into more sin than the pagan nations ever did.
33.10: God tried to speak to Manasseh and the people, but they wasn't listening.
33.11: So God let the Assyrian army run up on them. They caught Manasseh with hooks, chained him up in bronze shackles, and dragged him to Babylon.
33.12: While he was locked up, Manasseh finally humbled himself and begged the God of his ancestors for help.
33.13: He prayed, and God actually listened. God brought him back to Jerusalem and restored him as king. That's when Manasseh finally realized the Lord was the true God.
33.14: After that, Manasseh built up a wall outside the City of David, all the way to the Fish Gate, and made it tall. He put commanders in all Judah's fortified cities.
33.15: He got rid of all the foreign gods, the idol he had set up in the Lord's temple, and the altars he had built in Jerusalem. He threw them out the city.
33.16: Then he repaired the altar of the Lord and started offering peace and thank offerings again. He ordered Judah to worship the Lord, the God of Israel.
33.17: The people still used the high places—but now they were using them for the Lord instead of idols.
33.18: Everything else Manasseh did—his story, his prayers, and the prophecies spoken to him—was recorded in the book of Israel's kings.
33.19: His prayer, how God listened, his sins, and where he built the idols before he got humble—it's all written in the book of Hozai.
33.20: Manasseh died and was buried in his own house. His son Amon took the throne after him.
33.21: Amon was 22 when he became king, and he only reigned for two years in Jerusalem.
33.22: He did evil too—just like his dad before the change. He kept serving the same idols Manasseh had made.
33.23: But unlike his father, Amon didn't humble himself. He just kept getting worse and worse.
33.24: His own servants plotted and killed him right in his house.
33.25: But the people of the land rose up, executed the conspirators, and put Amon's son Josiah on the throne.

34.1: Josiah was just 8 years old when he became king, and he ruled for 31 years in Jerusalem.
34.2: He did what was right in the Lord's eyes, just like David. He stayed focused—didn't veer left or right.
34.3: In the 8th year of his reign—still a youngin—he started seriously seekin' God. By year 12, he was on a mission. He tore down every high place, idol, and altar in Judah and Jerusalem.
34.4: He smashed the Baal altars right in front of him. Cut down the incense spots, broke the wooden, carved, and molded images to dust, and scattered it over the graves of the folks who used 'em.
34.5: He even burned the bones of those idol priests on their own altars—cleansing Judah and Jerusalem from top to bottom.
34.6: And he didn't stop there—he did the same in Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, Naphtali, and all around—swingin' axes.
34.7: After crushin' altars and images all across Israel, he came back to Jerusalem.
34.8: In the 18th year of his reign, after cleaning up the land and the temple, Josiah sent Shaphan, Maaseiah the city governor, and Joah the record keeper to fix up the Lord's temple.
34.9: They gave the money collected from the Levites at the temple—donations from all over: Manasseh, Ephraim, the remnant of Israel, Judah, Benjamin, and back in Jerusalem.
34.10: The funds went straight to the supervisors and then to the workers rebuilding and restoring God's house.
34.11: Craftsmen and builders used it to buy stone and timber for repairs, since the kings before had let things fall apart.
34.12: The workers were faithful. Overseers from the Levites—Jahath, Obadiah, Zechariah, Meshullam—kept things moving.
34.13: Other Levites, skilled in music, handled logistics, supervision, and admin work. Scribes, officers, gatekeepers—everyone had a role.
34.14: While they were handling the money, Hilkiah the priest found the Book of the Law from Moses.
34.15: He told Shaphan, "Yo, I found the Book of the Law in the temple!" and handed it to him.
34.16: Shaphan brought it to the king and said, "Everything you told us to do, we're doing.
34.17: The money's been collected and handed off properly."
34.18: Then he added, "Hilkiah gave me this book," and started reading it out loud.
34.19: When Josiah heard the words of the Law, he tore his clothes—he knew they'd fallen way off.
34.20: He told Hilkiah, Ahikam, Abdon, Shaphan, and Asaiah,
34.21: "Go talk to the Lord for me and the rest of the people. We messed up. God's anger is real 'cause our ancestors didn't follow His Word."
34.22: So they went to Huldah the prophetess—wife of Shallum, keeper of the wardrobe. She lived in Jerusalem's Second Quarter. They told her everything.
34.23: She said, "This is what God says:
34.24: 'I'm about to bring disaster on this place and everybody in it. Everything you read in that book is comin'.'
34.25: 'They turned away from Me, burned incense to fake gods, made Me furious. My anger is comin' and it ain't stoppin.'"
34.26: "'But for the king of Judah—tell him this:
34.27: Since your heart was soft and you humbled yourself, tore your clothes, and cried out to Me when you heard My words, I heard you too,' says the Lord.
34.28: 'I'ma let you die in peace. You won't have to see the destruction with your own eyes.'" So they brought that message back to Josiah.
34.29: Josiah gathered all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem.
34.30: Then he went up to the temple with all the people—priests, Levites, everybody. And he read the entire Book of the Covenant out loud so everyone could hear it.
34.31: Standing in front of the crowd, the king made a public promise to God: "I'm gonna follow the Lord with all my heart and soul. I'm keepin' everything written in this book."
34.32: He made everybody in Jerusalem and Benjamin commit to that same covenant. And they followed through—serving the God of their ancestors.
34.33: Josiah wiped out all the idol worship from the entire land that belonged to Israel. He made sure everybody stayed faithful to the Lord as long as he lived.

35.1: Josiah threw a massive Passover for the Lord in Jerusalem. They killed the lambs on the 14th day of the first month.
35.2: He set the priests up in their proper roles and encouraged them to stay strong in serving the Lord's house.
35.3: Then he told the Levites—those who taught the people and were dedicated to God—"Put the ark back in the temple Solomon built. Y'all don't need to carry it anymore. Focus on serving the Lord and His people now."
35.4: "Get ready by your family groups and divisions, just like David and Solomon laid out."
35.5: "Take your place in the temple and help the lay people line up by their family divisions too."
35.6: "Kill the Passover offerings, consecrate yourselves, and help your brothers follow God's Word just like Moses commanded."
35.7: Josiah gave out 30,000 lambs and young goats, plus 3,000 cattle—all from his own stash—for everyone there to use in the Passover.
35.8: His officials also gave generously to the people, priests, and Levites. Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel gave 2,600 animals and 300 cattle to the priests.
35.9: The Levite leaders—Conaniah, Shemaiah, Nethanel, Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad—gave 5,000 lambs and 500 cattle to their fellow Levites.
35.10: Everything was ready. The priests were in their positions, the Levites in their divisions, just like Josiah said.
35.11: They slaughtered the lambs, the priests sprinkled the blood, and the Levites handled the skinning.
35.12: The burnt offerings were handed out to the families so they could present them to the Lord—same for the cattle.
35.13: They roasted the lambs just like the law says. The other holy offerings were boiled or cooked, then quickly handed out to the people.
35.14: After all that, the Levites took care of food for themselves and for the priests—'cause the priests had been sacrificing all day and into the night.
35.15: The singers (Asaph's descendants) stayed in their spots, just like David, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun had commanded. The gatekeepers stayed at their gates too, since the Levites made sure they were fed.
35.16: The whole Passover and the burnt offerings were done in one day—just like Josiah ordered.
35.17: Everyone who came—Israelites and Judahites—kept Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven full days.
35.18: That Passover hit different—hadn't been one like it since Samuel's time. Not one king before Josiah had done it like this, with everyone involved.
35.19: And this all went down in Josiah's 18th year as king.
35.20: After all this, when Josiah had finished fixing up the temple, Egypt's king Necho came to fight at Carchemish near the Euphrates. Josiah tried to meet him in battle.
35.21: But Necho sent a message: "Yo, I ain't got beef with you, Judah. I'm on assignment from God to handle another enemy. Don't get in my way—you might end up fighting God Himself."
35.22: But Josiah wouldn't listen. He disguised himself and still went out to fight at Megiddo. He ignored the warning that came straight from God.
35.23: Archers hit Josiah. He told his servants, "I'm hurt bad. Get me outta here."
35.24: They took him from his chariot to another one and rushed him back to Jerusalem. He died and was buried in his family's tomb. The whole nation mourned hard for him.
35.25: The prophet Jeremiah even wrote a whole lament for Josiah. Singers still talk about it when they sing sad songs in Israel—it became a tradition, and it's all written down in the book of Laments.
35.26: Everything Josiah did—his good heart, his dedication to God's law—
35.27: All his actions from beginning to end are recorded in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.

36.1: After Josiah died, the people put his son Jehoahaz on the throne in Jerusalem.
36.2: He was 23 when he became king, but only lasted three months.
36.3: The king of Egypt came through, took him off the throne, and charged the land a heavy tax—100 talents of silver and 1 talent of gold.
36.4: Then Egypt made Jehoahaz's brother Eliakim king and changed his name to Jehoiakim. Meanwhile, Jehoahaz got taken back to Egypt.
36.5: Jehoiakim was 25 when he took over, and he ruled 11 years in Jerusalem. But he did evil in God's eyes.
36.6: Nebuchadnezzar from Babylon came for him—put him in chains and planned to drag him to Babylon.
36.7: Nebuchadnezzar also took some of the sacred items from God's temple and stored them in his own temple in Babylon.
36.8: The rest of Jehoiakim's messy reign is written in the book of the kings. Then his son Jehoiachin took the throne.
36.9: Jehoiachin was just 8 years old when he became king, and he ruled for 3 months and 10 days. He also did evil in God's sight.
36.10: When the new year came, Nebuchadnezzar summoned him, took him and the temple treasures to Babylon, and made Zedekiah king in his place.
36.11: Zedekiah was 21 when he became king and ruled for 11 years in Jerusalem.
36.12: But he did evil too—and didn't listen to the prophet Jeremiah, who was speaking straight from the Lord.
36.13: He even rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar after swearing an oath in God's name. Zedekiah stayed hard-headed and refused to turn back to God.
36.14: The leaders and the people kept spiraling deeper into sin, copying the filthy ways of the nations. They trashed God's temple, the very place He had made holy.
36.15: God kept sending messengers to warn them—early and often—'cause He cared for His people and His temple.
36.16: But they mocked the messengers, ignored the warnings, and laughed at the prophets—until God's anger hit a point of no return.
36.17: So He let the king of Babylon (the Chaldeans) come in and wreck shop. They killed young men in the temple itself, didn't spare anyone—old or young, strong or weak. God handed them all over.
36.18: The Babylonians took every treasure from God's temple, the king's palace, and the leaders. Everything got hauled off to Babylon.
36.19: They burned the temple down, tore down Jerusalem's walls, set the palaces on fire, and destroyed everything valuable.
36.20: Anyone who survived the massacre got taken to Babylon to be servants until Persia rose up.
36.21: This fulfilled what God told Jeremiah—the land finally got its rest. It lay desolate for 70 years to make up for all the ignored Sabbaths.
36.22: In Cyrus's first year as king of Persia, the Lord stirred up his spirit to fulfill Jeremiah's prophecy. Cyrus made an official proclamation across his kingdom, even wrote it down:
36.23: "This is what Cyrus king of Persia says: The Lord God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth. He told me to build Him a house in Jerusalem, in Judah. So who among y'all belongs to Him? May the Lord be with you—go on up!"
